doc.title: Al Grey interviewed by Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 3, 1995

title: Advice to students: school clinics, breathing and dynamics
summary: Grey talks about teaching feeling, breathing, Louis Armstrong's lip, lessons with John Coffey, and Basie's dynamics.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: Okay, now we’re coming just to the end of our hour-long tape that we have here. I’d like to ask you just one more question just for right now at any rate. And that is, if you had something that you wanted to say to students of music, and to the field of music as a whole, or to jazz more specifically, from your years of experience. Tell us some of the things that you think are important about the idiom and tell us in your own words how you feel oral culture is a part of jazz.

Jazz, well, you see you must look at it like this. They started having jazz artists to come in the schools and it hasn’t been that many years ago. And so they would bring Frank Foster and Basie’s band, we would come out and start doing clinics before concerts sometimes in schools, because we played many universities and colleges. So then Basie would pick me and Marshall for the saxes and Joe Newman for the trumpet, and we discovered that you get it in the books, you read it in the books, but to get the feeling of it, that’s not taught. You have to get that yourself. And so your teachers, they can’t teach that to you. So it’s very valuable to have someone to come in to class and even just show you how to breathe. Because I find that’s one of my biggest problems a lot of times with a trombone player, he’s blowing and he’s blowing, but there’s no one to tell Louis Armstrong how to blow his horn. And when he passed on, he had a big gash in his lip, a big gash, almost a quarter of an inch deep, where he kept pushing it in. So when I went to New England Conservatory of Music and had some lessons from John Coffey of the Boston Symphony, while I was in the Navy up there, I would get these lessons, you see? And he taught you to put all of this into your diaphragm and do it from the lip. Now also, what made Count Basie so great was he knew how to play, where we played “Little Darlin’” so soft. They don’t have the time to teach you about dynamics that much. Although you have pf or double p or f, double f or three f, you see? And they mark it on the paper, but if you have no experience of doing this, you’re going to have to play on the same level. So Basie could say “whisper here” and all of a sudden we had this “All of Me” [humms]. And out of that, anybody talking, you just jumped out of your seat just from that one bar [humms]. All the way back down to complete, and that’s not easy, you have to learn about those things. So anyone you see, and then you see if you’re supposed to be playing in this section and then you’re supposed to get louder and you’re supposed to come back, you start completely playing attention to your dynamics.
